open_obligations: Check that both error analyses use comparable tagging schemes.
Note that Michael et al. also attribute 33% of errors to judges ending early, which Khan et al.'s fixed-round design cannot show.
Check sample sizes of incorrect judgements in each study.
out.other_title: Debate errors: 33% from judges ending early, 46% from honest debater missing evidence
out.rationale: Michael et al. report 46% of incorrectly judged human debates involve the correct debater missing an important argument or piece of evidence (and 33% the judge ending early). Khan et al. report the most common human-judge error in LLM debate is weak arguments from the correct debater, usually poor choice of quotes, and take their LLM debaters to be the bottleneck; Michael et al.'s debaters are mostly expert humans, Khan et al.'s are GPT-4-Turbo.
out.scope: proposed SUPPORTS: what causes human judges to err in QuALITY debates: weak arguments or missed evidence from the honest debater

text: From reading transcripts and judge explanations for all cases where a human judge chose the incorrect answer, the paper reports that in debate the most common error is weak arguments from the correct debater, usually due to poor choice of quotes, which the authors take to mean their LLM debaters are far from optimal and are the bottleneck for higher judge accuracy. In consultancy the most common error is the judge failing to elicit key quotes from the incorrect consultant.
title: Most common human debate error: weak arguments from the correct LLM debater
